---- MODULE W4Od9m2p6t3 ----
EXTENDS Naturals

CONSTANTS Participant, MaxEpoch

VARIABLES epoch, phase, vote, partEpoch, shedEpoch

vars == <<epoch, phase, vote, partEpoch, shedEpoch>>

\* epoch/phase model a 2PC round run by the grid operator over feeder shedding.
\* partEpoch[p] is the last round p has synced with -- a slow p may lag behind.
\* shedEpoch[p] records the round p last actually shed load in (0 = never).
\* AuthorizedShedOnly: a shed recorded for the live round must be backed by an
\* in-round sync and a yes vote, i.e. no stale or unauthorized shed action.

TypeOK ==
    /\ epoch \in 0..MaxEpoch
    /\ phase \in {"idle", "prepare", "committed", "aborted"}
    /\ vote \in [Participant -> {"none", "yes", "no"}]
    /\ partEpoch \in [Participant -> 0..MaxEpoch]
    /\ shedEpoch \in [Participant -> 0..MaxEpoch]

Init ==
    /\ epoch = 0
    /\ phase = "idle"
    /\ vote = [p \in Participant |-> "none"]
    /\ partEpoch = [p \in Participant |-> 0]
    /\ shedEpoch = [p \in Participant |-> 0]

StartRound ==
    /\ phase = "idle"
    /\ epoch < MaxEpoch
    /\ epoch' = epoch + 1
    /\ phase' = "prepare"
    /\ vote' = [p \in Participant |-> "none"]
    /\ UNCHANGED <<partEpoch, shedEpoch>>

Sync(p) ==
    /\ partEpoch[p] < epoch
    /\ partEpoch' = [partEpoch EXCEPT ![p] = epoch]
    /\ UNCHANGED <<epoch, phase, vote, shedEpoch>>

CastVote(p, v) ==
    /\ phase = "prepare"
    /\ partEpoch[p] = epoch
    /\ vote[p] = "none"
    /\ vote' = [vote EXCEPT ![p] = v]
    /\ UNCHANGED <<epoch, phase, partEpoch, shedEpoch>>

Commit ==
    /\ phase = "prepare"
    /\ \A p \in Participant : vote[p] = "yes"
    /\ phase' = "committed"
    /\ UNCHANGED <<epoch, vote, partEpoch, shedEpoch>>

Abort ==
    /\ phase = "prepare"
    /\ \E p \in Participant : vote[p] = "no"
    /\ phase' = "aborted"
    /\ UNCHANGED <<epoch, vote, partEpoch, shedEpoch>>

Shed(p) ==
    /\ phase = "committed"
    /\ partEpoch[p] = epoch
    /\ vote[p] = "yes"
    /\ shedEpoch' = [shedEpoch EXCEPT ![p] = epoch]
    /\ UNCHANGED <<epoch, phase, vote, partEpoch>>

ResetRound ==
    /\ phase \in {"committed", "aborted"}
    /\ phase' = "idle"
    /\ UNCHANGED <<epoch, vote, partEpoch, shedEpoch>>

Next ==
    \/ StartRound
    \/ \E p \in Participant : Sync(p)
    \/ \E p \in Participant, v \in {"yes", "no"} : CastVote(p, v)
    \/ Commit
    \/ Abort
    \/ \E p \in Participant : Shed(p)
    \/ ResetRound

Spec == Init /\ [][Next]_vars

AuthorizedShedOnly ==
    \A p \in Participant :
        (epoch > 0 /\ shedEpoch[p] = epoch) => (partEpoch[p] = epoch /\ vote[p] = "yes")

====

SPECIFICATION Spec
CONSTANTS
    p1 = p1
    p2 = p2
    p3 = p3
    Participant = {p1, p2, p3}
    MaxEpoch = 3
INVARIANT AuthorizedShedOnly
CHECK_DEADLOCK FALSE
nl:
A regional power-grid operator runs a two-phase-commit protocol across a small set of substation controllers to decide whether to shed load on a feeder during a demand spike. Each round, the operator (acting as coordinator) opens a new epoch, asking every substation controller to vote "yes" (able to shed safely) or "no" (must stay online) for that specific epoch. A controller may only cast a vote once it has synchronized its local epoch counter with the operator's current epoch -- a controller that has not yet synchronized is considered stale for that round and is barred from voting or acting.

Only if every controller votes "yes" does the operator move the round to "committed"; if any controller votes "no", the round is "aborted" instead. Feeder shedding -- the actual physical action of cutting load -- is only performed by a controller that is both caught up to the live epoch and holds a "yes" vote recorded for that same epoch. Once a round resolves (committed or aborted), the operator resets to idle and may open the next epoch. Controllers synchronize asynchronously and independently: a controller can be slow to catch up to the current epoch (it may sit stale for a while before syncing), but it never crashes or drops out permanently -- it always eventually catches up if given the chance, it just cannot be assumed to act promptly.

This models the real hazard in feeder-shedding coordination: a controller that missed the current round's vote (because it was still processing the prior epoch) must never shed load on the strength of an old, no-longer-valid authorization, and a controller that never actually voted "yes" this round must never act as though it had.

The full action set is: StartRound (operator opens a new epoch and clears votes), Sync (a controller catches up its local epoch to the operator's current epoch), CastVote (a synchronized controller records a yes/no vote for the live epoch), Commit (operator moves to committed once all votes are yes), Abort (operator moves to aborted once any vote is no), Shed (a synchronized, yes-voting controller actually cuts load for the live epoch), and ResetRound (operator returns to idle after a round resolves).
SAFETY PROPERTY: whenever a controller's recorded shed-epoch equals the operator's current live epoch, that controller must actually be synchronized to the live epoch and hold a yes-vote for it -- no stale or unauthorized controller ever performs the shed action.

---- MODULE W4Od18m7p1t0 ----
EXTENDS Naturals

CONSTANTS Hub, MaxVer

VARIABLES schedVer, schedule, lastSeen, commitAt, down, wantsAdd

vars == <<schedVer, schedule, lastSeen, commitAt, down, wantsAdd>>

\* schedVer/schedule form the CAS register: a hub may only join schedule when
\* its lastSeen snapshot still matches the live schedVer token.
\* commitAt[h] records the token value at which h's own addition landed --
\* NoLostUpdate below checks that no two hubs ever share that token.

TypeOK ==
    /\ schedVer \in 0..MaxVer
    /\ schedule \subseteq Hub
    /\ lastSeen \in [Hub -> 0..MaxVer]
    /\ commitAt \in [Hub -> 0..MaxVer]
    /\ down \in [Hub -> BOOLEAN]
    /\ wantsAdd \in [Hub -> BOOLEAN]

Init ==
    /\ schedVer = 1
    /\ schedule = {}
    /\ lastSeen = [h \in Hub |-> 0]
    /\ commitAt = [h \in Hub |-> 0]
    /\ down = [h \in Hub |-> FALSE]
    /\ wantsAdd = [h \in Hub |-> FALSE]

Request(h) ==
    /\ ~down[h]
    /\ ~wantsAdd[h]
    /\ wantsAdd' = [wantsAdd EXCEPT ![h] = TRUE]
    /\ UNCHANGED <<schedVer, schedule, lastSeen, commitAt, down>>

SyncHub(h) ==
    /\ ~down[h]
    /\ wantsAdd[h]
    /\ commitAt[h] = 0
    /\ lastSeen' = [lastSeen EXCEPT ![h] = schedVer]
    /\ UNCHANGED <<schedVer, schedule, commitAt, down, wantsAdd>>

AddCode(h) ==
    /\ ~down[h]
    /\ wantsAdd[h]
    /\ commitAt[h] = 0
    /\ lastSeen[h] = schedVer
    /\ schedVer < MaxVer
    /\ schedule' = schedule \cup {h}
    /\ schedVer' = schedVer + 1
    /\ commitAt' = [commitAt EXCEPT ![h] = schedVer]
    /\ UNCHANGED <<lastSeen, down, wantsAdd>>

CrashHub(h) ==
    /\ ~down[h]
    /\ \A q \in Hub : ~down[q]
    /\ down' = [down EXCEPT ![h] = TRUE]
    /\ UNCHANGED <<schedVer, schedule, lastSeen, commitAt, wantsAdd>>

Next ==
    \/ \E h \in Hub : Request(h)
    \/ \E h \in Hub : SyncHub(h)
    \/ \E h \in Hub : AddCode(h)
    \/ \E h \in Hub : CrashHub(h)

Spec == Init /\ [][Next]_vars /\ \A h \in Hub : WF_vars(SyncHub(h)) /\ WF_vars(AddCode(h))

NoLostUpdate ==
    \A h1, h2 \in Hub :
        (h1 # h2 /\ commitAt[h1] > 0 /\ commitAt[h2] > 0) => commitAt[h1] # commitAt[h2]

Progress == \A h \in Hub : wantsAdd[h] ~> (commitAt[h] > 0 \/ down[h])

====

SPECIFICATION Spec
CONSTANTS
    h1 = h1
    h2 = h2
    h3 = h3
    Hub = {h1, h2, h3}
    MaxVer = 4
INVARIANT NoLostUpdate
PROPERTY Progress
CHECK_DEADLOCK FALSE
nl:
A smart-home vendor runs several hub controllers (a front-door hub, a garage hub, a side-gate hub) that all share one access schedule: the set of guest door codes currently authorized in the house. Rather than a central coordinator, the hubs cooperate through a compare-and-swap register: the shared schedule carries a version token, and a hub wishing to add its own guest code must first take a snapshot of that token, then attempt to swap in the new schedule only if the token still matches its snapshot. If another hub updated the schedule first, the token has moved on and the swap is rejected, so the hub must re-snapshot the current token and try again -- this is exactly what prevents one hub's addition from silently clobbering another hub's already-committed addition.

Concretely, each hub starts idle and, at some point, decides it wants to add its own code to the shared schedule. From then on it repeatedly re-synchronizes its local snapshot of the version token until the token it has last seen matches the register's live token, at which point its compare-and-swap succeeds: the code joins the shared schedule, the token advances by one, and the hub records the exact token value at which its own addition landed. Because every successful swap bumps the token, no two hubs can ever believe they landed at the same token value -- each committed addition gets its own distinct, traceable slot, so updates are never lost or overwritten without a trace.

One hub in the whole network can, at any point, crash silently -- its firmware simply stops responding, with no notification to the others. A crashed hub takes no further actions ever again (in particular it never lands its own pending addition), but crucially the other hubs' snapshot-and-swap retries are completely unaffected by another hub's crash: they keep re-synchronizing and re-attempting until their own addition succeeds. The mechanism guarantees that any hub which wants to add its code, and which never crashes, eventually gets that addition durably recorded in the shared schedule.

The full action set is: Request (a hub decides it wants to add its own guest code to the shared schedule), SyncHub (a hub re-synchronizes its local snapshot of the register's version token to the current live value), AddCode (a hub whose snapshot matches the live token swaps its code into the shared schedule and the token advances), and CrashHub (the one hub in the network permitted to crash does so silently and takes no further action).
SAFETY PROPERTY: no two hubs ever have their additions recorded at the same version token -- every committed addition to the shared schedule lands at its own distinct token, so no hub's update is ever silently lost or overwritten by another's.
LIVENESS PROPERTY: every hub that has requested to add its code eventually either gets that addition durably recorded in the shared schedule or crashes -- a slow hub competing with others is never left waiting forever.

---- MODULE W4Od8m6p1t5 ----
EXTENDS Naturals

CONSTANTS Advisor, MaxTime, LeaseLen, MaxGen

VARIABLES clock, holder, expiry, gen, editedInGen

vars == <<clock, holder, expiry, gen, editedInGen>>

\* holder/expiry model the leased-ownership record; gen is bumped on every
\* hand-off (normal acquire or admin override), so each lease instance gets
\* its own generation stamp. editedInGen[a] records which generation a's
\* edit landed in -- NoLostUpdate checks those stamps are never shared.

TypeOK ==
    /\ clock \in 0..MaxTime
    /\ holder \in Advisor \cup {"none"}
    /\ expiry \in 0..(MaxTime + LeaseLen)
    /\ gen \in 0..MaxGen
    /\ editedInGen \in [Advisor -> 0..MaxGen]

Init ==
    /\ clock = 0
    /\ holder = "none"
    /\ expiry = 0
    /\ gen = 0
    /\ editedInGen = [a \in Advisor |-> 0]

Tick ==
    /\ clock < MaxTime
    /\ clock' = clock + 1
    /\ UNCHANGED <<holder, expiry, gen, editedInGen>>

AcquireLease(a) ==
    /\ holder = "none"
    /\ gen < MaxGen
    /\ holder' = a
    /\ expiry' = clock + LeaseLen
    /\ gen' = gen + 1
    /\ UNCHANGED <<clock, editedInGen>>

Edit(a) ==
    /\ holder = a
    /\ clock <= expiry
    /\ editedInGen' = [editedInGen EXCEPT ![a] = gen]
    /\ UNCHANGED <<clock, holder, expiry, gen>>

NaturalExpiry ==
    /\ holder # "none"
    /\ clock > expiry
    /\ holder' = "none"
    /\ UNCHANGED <<clock, expiry, gen, editedInGen>>

AdminOverride(a) ==
    /\ holder # a
    /\ gen < MaxGen
    /\ holder' = a
    /\ expiry' = clock + LeaseLen
    /\ gen' = gen + 1
    /\ UNCHANGED <<clock, editedInGen>>

Next ==
    \/ Tick
    \/ \E a \in Advisor : AcquireLease(a)
    \/ \E a \in Advisor : Edit(a)
    \/ NaturalExpiry
    \/ \E a \in Advisor : AdminOverride(a)

Spec == Init /\ [][Next]_vars

NoLostUpdate ==
    \A a1, a2 \in Advisor :
        (a1 # a2 /\ editedInGen[a1] > 0 /\ editedInGen[a2] > 0) => editedInGen[a1] # editedInGen[a2]

====

SPECIFICATION Spec
CONSTANTS
    a1 = a1
    a2 = a2
    a3 = a3
    Advisor = {a1, a2, a3}
    MaxTime = 5
    LeaseLen = 2
    MaxGen = 5
INVARIANT NoLostUpdate
CHECK_DEADLOCK FALSE
nl:
A university course-registration system lets several advisors edit one shared registration record for a course (its roster overrides: manual add/drop exceptions to the automated enrollment engine). Because two advisors editing the record at once could silently clobber each other's changes, the system uses lease-based ownership: an advisor must first acquire a lease on the record, which is only granted while no one else currently holds it, and the lease carries a fixed expiry measured against a shared clock. Only the current lease holder may commit an edit, and only while the shared clock has not yet passed the lease's expiry -- once the clock passes expiry, the lease lapses on its own and the record becomes free for the next advisor to claim.

Each time a lease is granted -- whether through the normal acquire path or through the registrar's admin override -- the system stamps a fresh lease generation number, and any edit an advisor commits is tagged with the generation under which it was made. This generation tag is what protects against lost updates: because a new generation is stamped every time ownership changes hands, no two different advisors can ever have their edits tagged with the same generation, so no advisor's committed edit can ever be silently attributed to, or overwritten by, another advisor's turn with the record.

The registrar holds a privileged admin override: unlike an ordinary advisor, the registrar may force the lease directly onto a chosen advisor at any moment, regardless of who currently holds it or whether that lease has expired yet -- for example to break a session where an advisor's client has hung. The override still goes through the same generation-stamping path as a normal acquire, so the protection against lost updates holds even when the registrar exercises this privileged power.

The full action set is: Tick (the shared clock advances by one), AcquireLease (an advisor claims the record's lease once it is free, stamping a new generation and expiry), Edit (the current lease holder commits an edit tagged with the live generation, only while the clock has not passed expiry), NaturalExpiry (the lease lapses on its own once the clock passes its expiry, freeing the record), and AdminOverride (the registrar forcibly hands the lease to a chosen advisor at any time, stamping a new generation regardless of the current holder or expiry).
SAFETY PROPERTY: no two different advisors ever have committed edits tagged with the same lease generation -- every committed edit is attributable to exactly the one advisor who held that generation's lease, so updates are never lost or silently overwritten.

---- MODULE W4Od7m7p5t3 ----
EXTENDS Naturals

CONSTANTS Crane, Container, MaxTok

VARIABLES tok, claimant, hoistedBy, held, snap

vars == <<tok, claimant, hoistedBy, held, snap>>

\* tok/claimant form the per-container CAS claim register; a crane's snap must
\* still match the live tok for its claim to win. hoistedBy[k] latches the one
\* crane that actually performed the irreversible lift for container k.
\* AtMostOnceHoist ties hoistedBy back to the winning claimant, which also
\* pins the lift to happening exactly once (hoistedBy never resets).

TypeOK ==
    /\ tok \in [Container -> 0..MaxTok]
    /\ claimant \in [Container -> Crane \cup {"none"}]
    /\ hoistedBy \in [Container -> Crane \cup {"none"}]
    /\ held \in [Crane -> Container \cup {"none"}]
    /\ snap \in [Crane -> 0..MaxTok]

Init ==
    /\ tok = [k \in Container |-> 0]
    /\ claimant = [k \in Container |-> "none"]
    /\ hoistedBy = [k \in Container |-> "none"]
    /\ held = [c \in Crane |-> "none"]
    /\ snap = [c \in Crane |-> 0]

PickTarget(c, k) ==
    /\ held[c] = "none"
    /\ hoistedBy[k] = "none"
    /\ claimant[k] = "none"
    /\ held' = [held EXCEPT ![c] = k]
    /\ snap' = [snap EXCEPT ![c] = tok[k]]
    /\ UNCHANGED <<tok, claimant, hoistedBy>>

ClaimCAS(c) ==
    LET k == held[c] IN
        /\ held[c] # "none"
        /\ claimant[k] = "none"
        /\ snap[c] = tok[k]
        /\ tok[k] < MaxTok
        /\ claimant' = [claimant EXCEPT ![k] = c]
        /\ tok' = [tok EXCEPT ![k] = tok[k] + 1]
        /\ UNCHANGED <<held, snap, hoistedBy>>

Hoist(c) ==
    LET k == held[c] IN
        /\ held[c] # "none"
        /\ claimant[k] = c
        /\ hoistedBy[k] = "none"
        /\ hoistedBy' = [hoistedBy EXCEPT ![k] = c]
        /\ UNCHANGED <<tok, claimant, held, snap>>

ReleaseDone(c) ==
    LET k == held[c] IN
        /\ held[c] # "none"
        /\ hoistedBy[k] # "none"
        /\ held' = [held EXCEPT ![c] = "none"]
        /\ UNCHANGED <<tok, claimant, hoistedBy, snap>>

Abandon(c) ==
    LET k == held[c] IN
        /\ held[c] # "none"
        /\ claimant[k] # "none"
        /\ claimant[k] # c
        /\ held' = [held EXCEPT ![c] = "none"]
        /\ UNCHANGED <<tok, claimant, hoistedBy, snap>>

Next ==
    \/ \E c \in Crane, k \in Container : PickTarget(c, k)
    \/ \E c \in Crane : ClaimCAS(c)
    \/ \E c \in Crane : Hoist(c)
    \/ \E c \in Crane : ReleaseDone(c)
    \/ \E c \in Crane : Abandon(c)

Spec ==
    /\ Init /\ [][Next]_vars
    /\ \A c \in Crane, k \in Container : SF_vars(PickTarget(c, k))
    /\ \A c \in Crane : WF_vars(ClaimCAS(c)) /\ WF_vars(Hoist(c))
                        /\ WF_vars(ReleaseDone(c)) /\ WF_vars(Abandon(c))

AtMostOnceHoist ==
    \A k \in Container : hoistedBy[k] # "none" => hoistedBy[k] = claimant[k]

Progress == \A k \in Container : <>(hoistedBy[k] # "none")

====

SPECIFICATION Spec
CONSTANTS
    c1 = c1
    c2 = c2
    k1 = k1
    k2 = k2
    Crane = {c1, c2}
    Container = {k1, k2}
    MaxTok = 1
INVARIANT AtMostOnceHoist
PROPERTY Progress
CHECK_DEADLOCK FALSE
nl:
A container-ship crane yard operates several gantry cranes that compete for the job of hoisting containers off an incoming vessel. Each container on the ship has its own claim register: a compare-and-swap token that starts at zero. A crane that wants to service a container first moves into position and takes a snapshot of that container's current token. It then attempts a compare-and-swap claim: the claim succeeds, and the crane becomes the container's recorded claimant, only if no one else has claimed the container yet and the crane's snapshot still matches the register's live token (the token is bumped the instant a claim succeeds). If another crane's claim beat it to the register, the snapshot is now stale and the crane must abandon that container and move on to another one.

Only the crane recorded as a container's claimant may actually perform the hoist -- the physical, irreversible act of lifting the container off the ship. Once a container has been hoisted it can never be hoisted again, so the claim register's compare-and-swap step is what prevents two cranes from both believing they are clear to lift the same container at once. After a crane either completes its hoist or abandons a losing claim, it becomes free to move on and take aim at another still-unclaimed, unhoisted container.

Any crane in the yard can be arbitrarily slow -- it might sit in position for a long time before taking its snapshot, before attempting its claim, or before actually swinging into the hoist -- but no crane ever breaks down or drops out permanently; every crane that still has work available to it keeps making progress eventually, just not necessarily promptly. Because of this, the yard is guaranteed to eventually hoist every container exactly once, no matter how the cranes' relative speeds play out.

The full action set is: PickTarget (an idle crane moves onto an unclaimed, unhoisted container and snapshots its token), ClaimCAS (a crane whose snapshot still matches the live token wins the compare-and-swap claim on its target container), Hoist (the recorded claimant of a container performs the irreversible lift), ReleaseDone (a crane that finished hoisting its container becomes idle again), and Abandon (a crane whose target was claimed by someone else gives up on it and becomes idle again).
SAFETY PROPERTY: whenever a container has actually been hoisted, the crane credited with hoisting it is exactly the crane that legitimately won that container's compare-and-swap claim -- the irreversible hoist can never be credited to, or performed by, any crane other than the recorded claimant, which also means it can only ever happen once per container.
LIVENESS PROPERTY: every container in the yard is eventually hoisted, regardless of how slowly any individual crane moves.

---- MODULE W4Od17m2p4t3 ----
EXTENDS Naturals

CONSTANTS Segment, Cap, StartLoad

VARIABLES occ, phase, src, dst, voteSrc, voteDst

vars == <<occ, phase, src, dst, voteSrc, voteDst>>

\* One 2PC round moves at most one bag between two belt segments. VoteDest
\* only votes yes if the destination has headroom under its fixed Cap --
\* that vote is what CapacityBound below is checking never gets bypassed.

TypeOK ==
    /\ occ \in [Segment -> Nat]
    /\ phase \in {"idle", "prepare", "commit", "abort"}
    /\ src \in Segment \cup {"none"}
    /\ dst \in Segment \cup {"none"}
    /\ voteSrc \in {"none", "yes", "no"}
    /\ voteDst \in {"none", "yes", "no"}

Init ==
    /\ occ = [s \in Segment |-> StartLoad]
    /\ phase = "idle"
    /\ src = "none"
    /\ dst = "none"
    /\ voteSrc = "none"
    /\ voteDst = "none"

StartTransfer(s, d) ==
    /\ phase = "idle"
    /\ s # d
    /\ phase' = "prepare"
    /\ src' = s
    /\ dst' = d
    /\ voteSrc' = "none"
    /\ voteDst' = "none"
    /\ UNCHANGED occ

VoteSource ==
    /\ phase = "prepare"
    /\ voteSrc = "none"
    /\ voteSrc' = (IF occ[src] >= 1 THEN "yes" ELSE "no")
    /\ UNCHANGED <<occ, phase, src, dst, voteDst>>

VoteDest ==
    /\ phase = "prepare"
    /\ voteDst = "none"
    /\ voteDst' = (IF occ[dst] < Cap THEN "yes" ELSE "no")
    /\ UNCHANGED <<occ, phase, src, dst, voteSrc>>

Commit ==
    /\ phase = "prepare"
    /\ voteSrc = "yes"
    /\ voteDst = "yes"
    /\ phase' = "commit"
    /\ occ' = [occ EXCEPT ![src] = @ - 1, ![dst] = @ + 1]
    /\ UNCHANGED <<src, dst, voteSrc, voteDst>>

Abort ==
    /\ phase = "prepare"
    /\ (voteSrc = "no" \/ voteDst = "no")
    /\ phase' = "abort"
    /\ UNCHANGED <<occ, src, dst, voteSrc, voteDst>>

ResetRound ==
    /\ phase \in {"commit", "abort"}
    /\ phase' = "idle"
    /\ src' = "none"
    /\ dst' = "none"
    /\ voteSrc' = "none"
    /\ voteDst' = "none"
    /\ UNCHANGED occ

Next ==
    \/ \E s, d \in Segment : StartTransfer(s, d)
    \/ VoteSource
    \/ VoteDest
    \/ Commit
    \/ Abort
    \/ ResetRound

Spec == Init /\ [][Next]_vars

CapacityBound == \A s \in Segment : occ[s] <= Cap

====

SPECIFICATION Spec
CONSTANTS
    s1 = s1
    s2 = s2
    s3 = s3
    Segment = {s1, s2, s3}
    Cap = 2
    StartLoad = 1
INVARIANT CapacityBound
CHECK_DEADLOCK FALSE
nl:
An airport baggage router moves bags between conveyor-belt segments feeding the sorting hall, and it uses a two-phase-commit protocol to decide each single bag transfer between two segments. To move a bag from a source segment to a destination segment, the router first opens a transfer round: both the source and the destination segment are asked to vote. The source votes "yes" only if it actually still holds a bag to hand off; the destination votes "yes" only if accepting one more bag would not push its occupancy past its fixed belt capacity. Only when both segments vote "yes" does the router commit the round -- the bag count moves from source to destination -- otherwise the round is aborted and no bag moves.

This capacity check by the destination segment is the crux of the safety mechanism: a destination segment that is already at capacity must always vote "no," and it is exactly that vote that stops the transfer from ever pushing its occupancy over the limit. Once a round resolves (committed or aborted), the router returns to idle and may open a new transfer round between any pair of segments.

A segment can be slow to cast its vote in a round -- the router may wait an arbitrary amount of time for a segment's belt-load sensor to respond -- but a segment never goes offline or drops out of a round entirely; every vote it owes eventually gets cast, it simply cannot be assumed to respond promptly. The router never commits a transfer on partial information: both votes must actually be in before it decides, so a slow segment can delay a round but can never cause its capacity limit to be silently violated.

The full action set is: StartTransfer (the router opens a new round between a chosen source and destination segment), VoteSource (the source segment votes yes only if it currently holds a bag to give up), VoteDest (the destination segment votes yes only if accepting a bag would not exceed its belt capacity), Commit (the router moves the bag once both votes are yes), Abort (the router cancels the round once either vote is no), and ResetRound (the router returns to idle once a round has resolved).
SAFETY PROPERTY: no conveyor-belt segment's occupancy ever exceeds its fixed capacity.

---------------------------- MODULE W4Od3m3p4t3 ----------------------------
EXTENDS Naturals

CONSTANTS Banks, NoLeader, Capacity, MaxTerm

VARIABLES leader, term, slowFlag, batchCount, phase

vars == <<leader, term, slowFlag, batchCount, phase>>

TypeOK ==
  /\ leader \in Banks \cup {NoLeader}
  /\ term \in 0..MaxTerm
  /\ slowFlag \in BOOLEAN
  /\ batchCount \in 0..Capacity
  /\ phase \in {"open", "closing", "flushed"}

Init ==
  /\ leader = NoLeader
  /\ term = 0
  /\ slowFlag = FALSE
  /\ batchCount = 0
  /\ phase = "open"

ElectLeader ==
  /\ term < MaxTerm
  /\ (leader = NoLeader \/ slowFlag = TRUE)
  /\ \E b \in Banks :
       /\ leader' = b
       /\ term' = term + 1

The coordinator (whichever bank currently holds the role) may close the open batch at its discretion, moving it to a closing state; a closed batch is then flushed at the settlement window, after which a fresh batch is opened for the next cycle.

nl:
An airport's runway allocator decides which aircraft may use the single active runway next, and it must never let a second flight's clearance be finalized while an earlier flight's clearance for the same runway is still being resolved. Granting the runway goes through a two-phase commit across the controllers who must agree before a clearance is final: several aircraft may have open requests for the runway at once, and the radio and data links carrying each controller's vote back to the allocator do not guarantee delivery in the order the votes were cast, so votes and requests can arrive out of sequence.

To stay safe under this reordering, every request that opens is stamped with a fresh fencing term, a counter that only ever increases. Participants (the tower and approach control) cast their votes for a specific flight's request independently of one another and of any other flight's request, so the order in which votes and competing requests land is never fixed. A flight's clearance is only finalized once every participant has voted for it and its fencing term still matches the allocator's current term; if some other, later request has since advanced the term, the earlier request's votes -- however complete -- are recognized as stale and cannot be used to grant the runway, and that earlier request instead gives up so its flight can try again.

A flight holding the runway eventually vacates it, freeing the runway for the next clearance to be finalized. An open request that has been superseded does not linger forever: it is always eventually resolved, either by being granted the runway or by giving up once a newer request has taken over the fencing term.

The full action set is: Request (a flight opens a request for the runway, advancing the fencing term), Vote (a participant casts its vote for a specific flight's open request, independently of any other flight's request), Commit (a flight is granted the runway once every participant has voted for it and its fencing term is still current), Reset (an open request whose fencing term has been superseded by a later request gives up), and Release (a flight holding the runway gives it up).
SAFETY PROPERTY: Whenever the runway has a recorded holder, that holder's own fencing term must still equal the allocator's current term, so a clearance built on votes that a later request has already superseded can never be honored, and the runway can never be handed to a second flight while an earlier, now-stale claim is still being finalized.
LIVENESS PROPERTY: Every flight's open request eventually stops being open -- it is always eventually either granted the runway or superseded and given up, never stuck pending forever.

nl:
A hospital pharmacy's automated dispensing cabinet has exactly one mechanical arm that pulls medication from stock, and several pharmacist workstations can request it to fill a prescription. Only one workstation may actually be driving the arm at any moment, because two workstations moving it at once would risk mis-picking or double-dispensing a controlled substance. Access to the arm is arbitrated by a compare-and-swap register: a workstation may only begin dispensing by atomically swapping the register from "free" to its own identity, and that swap succeeds for at most one workstation at a time.

A workstation that has won the register and is actively dispensing can become slow -- its scanner might be re-verifying a barcode, or its screen waiting on a confirmation -- without ever being treated as crashed or failed. A slow workstation still holds the register exactly as it did before; nothing about the arbitration changes because a holder is slow, and no other workstation is ever allowed to force its way in or treat the register as free just because the current holder is taking its time.

A workstation that requested the arm but has not yet won the compare-and-swap may also give up and step back to idle. Once a workstation finishes dispensing, it releases the register, which then becomes free for the next successful swap, and the count of prescriptions it has filled increases.

The full action set is: RequestLock (a workstation moves from idle to waiting on the arm), CASAcquire (a waiting workstation's compare-and-swap on the register succeeds because the register is currently free, and it begins dispensing), MarkSlow (a workstation currently dispensing is flagged as running slow, without losing the register), ReleaseLock (a dispensing workstation releases the register, freeing it and recording the completed prescription), and Abandon (a waiting workstation gives up and returns to idle before ever acquiring the register).
SAFETY PROPERTY: Any workstation that is actively dispensing must be the one currently holding the compare-and-swap register, so the register's mutual exclusion is never violated even while a holder is running slow.

The scheme has a hard capacity on how many blocks may be shed at once, because shedding beyond that threshold would itself destabilize downstream feeders that depend on partial supply continuing to flow.

Coordination is decided by an election with failover: at the start no substation coordinates, so any of them may take the role. A lagging coordinator is never treated as failed: its bookkeeping of shed blocks is untouched, so failover here is a hand-off of responsibility rather than a recovery from a crash.

While the grid is stable, the coordinator can order additional blocks shed, up to the capacity limit, and can also decide to begin restoring shed blocks. Once restoration begins, blocks are restored one at a time until none remain shed, at which point the grid returns to its stable state and a fresh stress cycle can begin.

    /\ taskHolder = [t \in Tasks |-> NoDrone]
    /\ taskEpoch = [t \in Tasks |-> 0]
    /\ droneGen = [d \in Drones |-> 0]

    /\ Cardinality(InFlight) < Capacity
    /\ taskStatus' = [taskStatus EXCEPT ![t] = "queued"]
    /\ UNCHANGED << taskHolder, taskEpoch, droneGen, crashed >>

    /\ taskHolder[t] = d
    /\ d \notin crashed
    /\ taskEpoch[t] = droneGen[d]
    /\ taskStatus' = [taskStatus EXCEPT ![t] = "done"]

    /\ taskHolder[t] \in crashed
    /\ taskEpoch[t] < droneGen[taskHolder[t]]

    /\ taskHolder' = [taskHolder EXCEPT ![t] = NoDrone]

CONSTANTS

    Tasks = {t1, t2, t3}
    Capacity = 2

PROPERTY AllTasksEventuallyDone
nl:
A small swarm of surveillance drones patrols a wildfire perimeter, reporting hotspots that must be inspected up close. Ground control keeps the inspection requests in a bounded work queue: a request first sits in an unbounded backlog, and control admits it into the small active queue only while the number of requests currently queued-or-in-progress is below the queue's fixed capacity. This backpressure keeps at most a handful of inspection jobs in flight at once, so a burst of new hotspots cannot overwhelm the swarm's limited bandwidth. Once a job is in the active queue, any drone that is not currently known to be down may pick it up and start flying the inspection.

Because the radio link is unreliable, ground control never learns instantly that a drone has crashed -- one drone, and only one, can go silently unresponsive mid-flight without announcing anything. Each drone carries its own fencing generation number, which starts at zero and is bumped the moment control detects that particular drone has crashed. Every job a drone picks up keeps a stamp equal to that drone's generation at pickup time, so a job's stamp only ever goes stale relative to its own holder's generation, never because some unrelated healthy drone happened to crash. Only a job whose stamp still equals its holder's live generation may be reported complete by that holder. A job orphaned because its holder's generation moved past its stamp is reclaimed back into the active queue -- with its holder cleared -- so a still-healthy drone can pick it up fresh and carry the inspection through to completion.

The full action set is: control admits a backlogged job into the active queue while under capacity, a non-crashed drone picks up a queued job and stamps it with its own live generation, a drone reports a job it holds complete (only while its stamp still matches its own live generation and it is not crashed), the one drone that ever crashes does so silently and its own generation is bumped, and an orphaned job whose stamp has gone stale relative to its crashed holder's generation is reclaimed back into the queue.
SAFETY PROPERTY: Whenever a job's recorded holder is a drone now known to be crashed, that job's stamp is already stale relative to that holder's own generation, so no unauthorized or stale drone can have its completion of that job accepted.
LIVENESS PROPERTY: Every inspection job is eventually reported complete, even the ones orphaned by the one drone that crashed silently.

A subway line is divided into fixed signalling blocks, each a track segment that must never be occupied by more than one train's movement authority at a time. A small pool of interlocking controllers takes turns being the one "signaller" in charge of granting block authority; a controller campaigns for the signaller seat only while it is vacant, and any campaigning controller may then take over the seat and begin a new operating cycle. The current signaller can go down at any time, immediately vacating the seat and clearing any pending campaigns, so a healthy controller can campaign and take over the moment that happens. Only the current signaller may grant a waiting train authority over a block, and it only ever grants a block that no other train currently holds; a train that has cleared a block releases it explicitly once it has fully passed through, and that release is the only way a block ever becomes free again.

Crucially, a train that is simply running behind schedule is not the same as a train that has failed. Operations staff can flag a train as running slow, or clear that flag once it catches back up, purely for monitoring and scheduling purposes -- this status has no bearing whatsoever on block authority. There is no timeout or forced-reclaim mechanism: a slow train keeps whatever block it holds for as long as it needs, and the signaller can never grant that same block out from under it just because the train is taking a long time. A stock exchange runs a single opening auction batch across a handful of listed symbols, and a small pool of matching engines forms the current configuration responsible for working that batch. Every symbol's opening-auction slot starts pending; any engine that belongs to the current configuration epoch may claim a pending slot, stamping it with that same epoch number, and the engine that holds a slot under the still-current epoch may report the auction for that symbol matched, which is final for the day. Membership in the configuration is epoch-numbered: engines are added or removed only by a reconfiguration event that also bumps the epoch number, so every claim ever made carries the exact epoch under which it was granted.

One matching engine can crash silently mid-batch, with no immediate signal to anyone. Detection is a separate step: only once the exchange's coordinator notices the crash does it run a reconfiguration, which bumps the epoch and drops the crashed engine from the active configuration in the same step. Any symbol slot still recorded as claimed by an engine that reconfiguration has just dropped is now carrying a stale epoch stamp, so it is reclaimed back to pending -- freeing it for a still-active engine to claim afresh under the new epoch rather than leaving it double-claimed by an engine the configuration no longer recognizes. A reconfiguration bumps the epoch for every outstanding claim, including ones held by engines that were never at fault, so an engine that is still very much active simply re-affirms its own claim under the new epoch number rather than losing its slot.

The full action set is: an engine crashes silently, the coordinator reconfigures -- bumping the epoch and dropping any crashed engine from the active configuration, an active engine claims a pending symbol slot under the current epoch, an active engine reports a symbol slot it claimed under the current epoch as matched, a symbol slot whose claimed owner has fallen out of the active configuration is reclaimed back to pending, and a still-active engine renews its own claim on a slot to bring its epoch stamp back up to date after a reconfiguration.
SAFETY PROPERTY: Whenever a symbol slot is still recorded as claimed by an engine no longer in the active configuration, that claim's epoch stamp is already stale relative to the live epoch, so the slot can never remain validly double-claimed by an engine the configuration has dropped.
LIVENESS PROPERTY: Every symbol's opening auction is eventually reported matched, even for symbols orphaned by the one engine that crashed silently.

nl:
A fleet of warehouse robots shares a small set of storage bins, and a central coordinator leases out exclusive use of a bin to one robot at a time rather than handing out a permanent claim. When the coordinator grants a free bin to a robot it stamps that lease with a fresh fencing token -- a number that strictly increases every time the bin changes hands -- and starts a bounded expiry countdown; it then sends the robot an asynchronous grant confirmation carrying that same token. The warehouse's wireless mesh does not guarantee in-order delivery, so that confirmation can arrive late, and only once it actually arrives does the robot itself come to believe it holds the bin. A robot may have only one lease request outstanding or confirmed at a time. Only a robot that has itself received confirmation of holding a bin may renew its expiry countdown or explicitly release the bin back to the pool; an unrenewed lease also lapses on its own once the bounded clock passes its expiry, which likewise bumps the bin's fencing token.

Because confirmations can be reordered, a message that finally arrives after its lease has already lapsed or been superseded must be recognized as stale rather than blindly applied: the robot checks the token the confirmation carries against the bin's current fencing token, and only accepts the confirmation -- registering itself as the bin's holder -- when the two still match. A confirmation whose token no longer matches the bin's current token is simply discarded, since the bin has since moved on to a new lease (or expired) under a newer token. This fencing check is what stops a late, reordered confirmation from one robot's already-superseded lease attempt from ever being accepted alongside a different robot's genuinely current lease on that same bin.

The full action set is: the coordinator grants a free bin to a robot with no outstanding request, bumping the bin's fencing token and queuing an asynchronous grant confirmation; a queued grant confirmation is delivered, possibly late or out of order, and is applied only if its token still matches the bin's current token; a confirmed robot renews its bin's expiry countdown; a confirmed robot releases its bin back to the pool; an unrenewed lease expires on its own once the clock passes its expiry, bumping the bin's fencing token; and the bounded clock ticks forward.
SAFETY PROPERTY: No two distinct robots ever simultaneously believe they hold the same storage bin, even when a late or reordered grant confirmation is finally delivered.

A vending machine network operates across a shopping mall, with several machines sharing
a single manufacturer's jackpot promotion: exactly one physical prize unit exists
somewhere in the network's back stock, and any machine could end up being the one to
dispense it to a customer. Which machine gets to dispense the prize is decided by a
compare-and-swap register shared by all machines: a machine that sees the register is
unclaimed can atomically swap it from unclaimed to its own identifier, and only a machine
that holds the register in its own name may actually dispense the prize.

Because dispensing the prize is irreversible -- once it leaves the back stock it is gone
for good and can never be dispensed a second time -- the register permanently locks into
a done state the instant a machine dispenses it, so no further machine can ever swap into
ownership afterward.

The twist is that a machine can crash silently: it can go offline without notice, and if
it happens to be the machine currently holding the register, it never gets around to
dispensing the prize. When that happens, the rest of the network eventually notices the
stale claim and reclaims the register so that a working machine can pick it up. Only one
machine in the whole network is ever assumed to crash this way.

The full action set is: a machine attempts to compare-and-swap the register from
unclaimed to itself; a machine holding the register dispenses the jackpot item,
permanently locking the register; a machine crashes silently (bounded to at most one
crash across the network); the network reclaims a stale registration held by a crashed
machine and returns the register to unclaimed.

compare-and-swap register is permanently locked and no further machine can ever be
granted ownership or dispense it again.
LIVENESS PROPERTY: despite at most one machine crashing silently while holding the
register, the jackpot item is eventually dispensed by some machine in the network.

A hospital's operating-room scheduling system tracks which shift roster is currently
authorized to book procedures, using a reconfiguration epoch number that increases every
time the charge nurse reorganizes on-call coverage. Each proposed admission of a patient
into the operating room is stamped with the epoch the on-call scheduler currently
believes is active; if the hospital reconfigures coverage in the meantime, that stamp can
go stale before the admission is finalized.

Admitting a patient into the operating room -- putting them under anesthesia and
beginning the procedure -- is an irreversible action: it can happen for a given patient at
most once, ever. Under normal operation, the on-call scheduler may only finalize the
admission if its stamped proposal epoch still matches the currently active epoch; a stale
proposal left over from before a reconfiguration is simply ineligible to admit the
patient.

The twist is that the hospital's chief of surgery holds a privileged admin override: at
any time, whether or not a valid current-epoch proposal exists, the chief may force the
admission through directly. Even so, the override respects the same irreversibility rule
as everyone else -- it can only ever admit a patient who has not already been admitted,
and it stamps the admission with whatever epoch is active at the moment it fires.

The full action set is: the charge nurse reconfigures on-call coverage, advancing the
epoch; the on-call scheduler stamps a fresh admission proposal with the currently active
epoch; the scheduler finalizes the admission using a proposal whose stamped epoch still
matches the current epoch; the chief of surgery force-admits the patient through the
privileged override regardless of proposal freshness.

the reconfiguration epoch recorded for that one-time admission can never exceed the
hospital's currently active epoch, so the irreversible admission can never be
contradicted or repeated by epoch bookkeeping running backward.

A university course-registration system enrolls students into a capacity-limited seat
pool using a two-phase-commit protocol among the systems that must agree before a seat
changes hands: the department's seat-inventory system and the financial-aid office, both
of which the registrar's coordinator must hear from before finalizing a registration.
When a student's registration attempt begins, the coordinator moves exactly one seat out
of the course's available pool into escrow and asks every participant to vote on whether
the registration may proceed.

Each participant can be slow to respond -- perhaps its system is under load -- but it is
never simply broken or unreachable; it always eventually casts a vote of yes or no. If
every participant votes yes, the coordinator commits the transaction and the escrowed
seat becomes an enrolled seat. If any participant votes no (for example, a hold on the
student's account), the coordinator aborts the transaction and the escrowed seat returns
to the available pool. After a decision, the coordinator resets to idle and may open a
new registration round.

Because seats are never created or destroyed by this protocol -- a seat is only ever
available, held in escrow during a vote, or enrolled -- the total number of seats across
those three states must always equal the course's fixed capacity.

The full action set is: the coordinator opens a two-phase-commit round by escrowing one
available seat; a participant casts a yes vote; a participant casts a no vote; the
coordinator commits the round once every participant has voted yes, enrolling the
escrowed seat; the coordinator aborts the round once any participant has voted no,
returning the escrowed seat to the available pool; the coordinator resets to idle after a
decision so a new round can begin.
SAFETY PROPERTY: at every moment, the number of seats available plus the number of seats
enrolled plus the one seat held in escrow (if any) always equals the course's fixed total
capacity.
LIVENESS PROPERTY: every two-phase-commit round that is opened eventually reaches a
decision -- committed or aborted -- even though individual participants may be slow to
vote.

A regional library network uses a circulating authorization token to control which branch
may commit a reservation against the shared, network-wide catalog of a single
high-demand title. The token travels around a ring of participating branches; whichever
branch currently holds it is the only one allowed to place a hold on the shared catalog
on behalf of a patron, and every other branch must wait its turn.

The library's participating branches are not fixed: the network's capacity changes at
runtime as branches join or leave the token ring (a new branch opening, or an existing
branch temporarily withdrawing from the shared program). Whenever the ring's membership
changes, the network stamps a new generation number on the ring and immediately reclaims
any outstanding token, since a token issued under an earlier generation becomes stale the
moment membership changes -- even if the same branch was mid-turn holding it.

Only a branch that both currently belongs to the ring and holds a token stamped with the
ring's current generation may ever commit a reservation; a branch that has left the ring,
or that is still clutching a token from before the last membership change, has no
authority to touch the catalog. The ring's dispatcher only ever hands the token to a
branch that is presently a member.

The full action set is: a new branch joins the ring, bumping the generation and
reclaiming any outstanding token; an existing branch leaves the ring, bumping the
generation and reclaiming any outstanding token; the ring dispatcher grants the vacant
token to a current member, stamping it with the current generation; a branch holding a
token whose generation still matches the ring's current generation commits a reservation
against the shared catalog and releases the token.
SAFETY PROPERTY: whenever any branch holds the authorization token, that branch is
currently a member of the ring and its token's generation stamp matches the ring's
current generation, so no unauthorized or stale branch can ever act on the shared
catalog.

A multiplayer game lobby matchmaker coordinates several player clients that all want to
write to one shared resource: the lobby's match ledger, which records the final team
assignments for the next match. Only one client may ever hold write access to the ledger
at a time, and that exclusive access is granted by a single circulating token -- the
mechanism is a token ring, where the token is handed from client to client and whoever
holds it is the only one allowed to touch the ledger.

A client that wants to finalize match assignments first registers a request for the
token. Whenever the token is free, the matchmaker grants it to one of the currently
requesting clients, who then holds exclusive access, writes to the ledger, and
afterward releases the token back to the pool so another requester can be served. The
ring guarantees that, left running normally, it keeps rotating access among everyone who
is asking for it.

The twist is that one client can crash silently at any point -- mid-request or even while
holding the token -- without any warning to the rest of the ring. If the crashed client
was holding the token, the ring detects the stale hold and reclaims the token so the rest
of the group is not locked out forever; if the crashed client only had a pending request,
that request is simply dropped since a crashed client can never act on a grant anyway.

The full action set is: a client registers a request for the token; the matchmaker grants
the free token to one of the requesting, non-crashed clients; the holding client releases
the token after finishing its write to the ledger; a client crashes silently (bounded to
at most one crash across the whole ring), dropping any pending request it had; the ring
reclaims the token from a holder that has been marked crashed.
SAFETY PROPERTY: at most one client ever holds exclusive write access to the lobby's
match ledger at the same time.
LIVENESS PROPERTY: despite at most one client crashing silently, every client that
registers a request for the token eventually either receives exclusive access or has its
request dropped because it crashed -- no live client is starved of the ledger forever.

A regional vending-machine network keeps a central depot of a single snack product and a
small fleet of vending machines that draw stock from it. Restocking a machine is done by
a two-phase commit protocol so that a can is never left ambiguously "in flight": a
coordinator first prepares a transfer by reserving one physical unit out of the depot on
behalf of a target machine, then either commits that reservation (the unit is delivered
into the machine's own slot, ready to be bought) or aborts it (the unit is returned to the
depot untouched). Only after a transfer has committed can a customer actually purchase the
unit from that machine's slot.

Because the network is auditable, every physical unit of product must always be
accounted for in exactly one place: sitting in the central depot, reserved in transit
during phase one of a transfer, loaded in a machine's slot after phase two committed, or
already sold to a customer. Nothing in the protocol is allowed to manufacture a new unit
out of thin air or make one vanish, whether the transfer succeeds, is rolled back, or the
unit is finally sold.

The network operator holds a privileged admin override for emergencies (e.g. a jammed
slot sensor): instead of waiting for a normal commit to finish, the operator can force a
unit that is still only reserved in transit straight through to a completed sale,
short-circuiting the usual "commit into slot, then vend" sequence. Even this shortcut must
still move the same physical unit from the "in transit" bucket to the "sold" bucket -- it
may skip a step of the protocol, but it can never create or destroy product.

The full action set is: prepare a transfer (reserve one unit from the depot for a target
machine), commit a prepared transfer (deliver the reserved unit into the machine's slot),
abort a prepared transfer (return the reserved unit to the depot), vend (sell a unit
already loaded in a machine's slot to a customer), and the admin's forced vend (sell a
still-in-transit reserved unit directly, bypassing the commit step).
SAFETY PROPERTY: at every reachable state, the number of units in the depot, plus the
number of units currently reserved in transit, plus the number of units loaded in
machine slots, plus the number of units already sold, equals the network's fixed total
supply -- no unit is ever created or destroyed by prepare, commit, abort, vend, or the
admin override.

A blood-bank inventory tracker manages a single refrigerated storage bay that holds the
bank's only unit of a rare blood type. Hospital wards that need the unit go through a
two-phase commit protocol before they may physically open the bay: a ward first submits a
request that is queued if the bay is currently busy, then, once the bay is free, the bank
grants the ward a phase-one reservation on the bay. The ward must confirm the reservation
(phase two, the commit) before it is allowed to actually draw from the bay; after drawing,
the ward releases the bay, which becomes free again for the next queued ward. A ward may
also abandon a phase-one reservation without ever confirming it, freeing the bay again
with no draw having taken place.

Because the bay physically holds one unit and can only be opened by one ward's staff at a
time, at most one ward may hold a reservation on the bay at any moment -- this is a strict
mutual-exclusion resource, never shared or double-booked, no matter how many wards are
simultaneously waiting in the queue.

For emergencies (a ward's staff going unresponsive mid-procedure), the blood bank's
on-call director holds a privileged admin override: the director may reclaim the bay from
whichever ward currently holds it, in either phase, snapping it back to free immediately.
Because an override interrupting a live procedure is logged as an incident, the director's
overrides are rate-limited and stop being available once the incident log is full.

The full action set is: a ward joins the waiting queue for the bay, a queued ward is
granted the phase-one reservation once the bay is free, a reserving ward confirms into
phase-two commit, a committed ward releases the bay after drawing, a reserving ward aborts
its phase-one reservation without drawing, and the director's rate-limited admin override
reclaims the bay from its current holder.
SAFETY PROPERTY: at most one ward ever holds a reservation on the storage bay at the same
time, in either phase, regardless of how many wards are queued or how many overrides the
director has exercised.
LIVENESS PROPERTY: every ward that joins the waiting queue for the bay is eventually
granted the reservation on the bay, so no queued ward waits forever while the bay keeps
cycling between other wards.

A regional library runs a reservation system for a single high-demand title, and the
shared roster of active holds on that title is replicated across a small cluster of
branch controllers. Exactly one controller acts as custodian of the roster at a time, but
custodianship changes hands through leader election with failover: any controller can be
(re-)elected custodian at any moment, which represents the cluster detecting that the
previous custodian has stalled or gone silent and handing the role to a fresh one. Each
election stamps the newly elected controller with a strictly higher election term than any
term issued before it.

Because a network hiccup can leave a deposed custodian unaware that it has been replaced,
a controller may still attempt to write to the shared roster using whatever term it was
last stamped with. To avoid a lost update -- an old custodian's write silently overwriting
data that a newer custodian already committed -- the roster only accepts a write whose
presented term is at least as high as the term already recorded on the roster; a write
from a controller carrying a stale term is simply refused. A successful write (adding a
hold or releasing one) re-stamps the roster with the writing controller's term.

The library also adjusts the title's hold capacity at runtime, for example when a
duplicate copy is added to or pulled from circulation; capacity may be raised or lowered
at any time, as long as it never drops below the number of holds currently active on the
roster.

The full action set is: a controller is (re-)elected custodian, receiving a fresh
strictly-higher election term; a controller adds a hold to the roster, provided its
presented term is not stale and the roster has spare capacity; a controller releases a
hold from the roster, provided its presented term is not stale; and the library changes
the title's hold capacity to any value that still accommodates the currently active holds.
SAFETY PROPERTY: the election term stamped on the roster is always exactly equal to the
highest term any write has ever carried, so a stale write can never silently roll the
roster's recorded term backward and no committed update is ever lost underneath an older
one.

A university course-registration system exposes the number of open seats in a
high-demand section as a single shared compare-and-swap register. A student's
registration client first reads the register, taking a snapshot of the current seat
count. The client then submits a compare-and-swap: the write is only applied if the
register still holds exactly the value the client last saw. If some other student's
registration (or a course drop) has changed the register in the meantime, the
compare-and-swap is cleanly refused and the client must re-read and try again rather
than blindly overwrite -- this is what stops one student's successful registration from
silently clobbering, double-counting, or dropping another's.

A student's registration client can be arbitrarily slow between taking its snapshot and
submitting the compare-and-swap -- it might be paused, rate-limited, or just running on a
loaded laptop -- but it is never assumed to have crashed: given enough time it always
eventually submits its compare-and-swap and finds out, one way or another, whether it
succeeded. A student who is enrolled may later drop the section, which returns the seat
to the shared register.

The full action set is: a student reads the register and takes a snapshot of the current
seat count; a student's compare-and-swap succeeds because its snapshot still matches the
live register and a seat is open; a student's compare-and-swap is refused because the
register has since changed or no seat remains open; and an enrolled student drops the
section, returning the seat to the register.

enrolled students always equals the section's total seat count, so no compare-and-swap
ever silently drops or double-counts a seat that another registration already claimed or
released.
LIVENESS PROPERTY: every student whose compare-and-swap attempt is outstanding
eventually has that attempt resolved, either accepted or refused, however slowly their
client happens to run.

A container-ship crane yard assigns quay cranes to individual containers using
lease-based ownership: before a crane may touch a container it must hold a lease on it,
and every lease the yard's dispatcher hands out is stamped with a fencing token -- a
number that strictly increases every time any lease is issued, for any crane, for any
container. A crane remembers only the token from the lease it was last handed. The
dispatcher may re-issue a container's lease to a (possibly different) crane at any time
it judges the previous lease to have lapsed, which immediately stamps a fresh, higher
token onto that container, whether or not the previous crane has finished or even
noticed.

Physically lifting a container off the ship is irreversible, so a crane may only perform
that lift if the token it is carrying still matches the token currently stamped on the
container; if the dispatcher has since re-issued the container's lease to someone else,
the token on the container has moved on, and the crane's lift attempt is refused rather
than silently repeating the lift. A crane holding a still-current lease may instead just
stand down without lifting (its shift ends normally), and a crane holding a token it can
tell is already stale may likewise stand down without ever attempting the lift. A
container's lease is only re-issued while that container has not yet been lifted.

A crane can be arbitrarily slow between being handed a lease and actually attempting the
lift -- weather, traffic, an operator taking a break -- but it is never assumed to have
broken down; it always eventually does something with the lease it is holding, whether
that is lifting, standing down, or standing down because it notices its token is stale.

The full action set is: the dispatcher issues a fresh, higher-token lease on a not-yet-
lifted container to an idle crane; a crane carrying a still-current token lifts its
assigned container; a crane carrying a still-current token stands down without lifting;
and a crane carrying a token it recognizes as stale stands down without lifting.
SAFETY PROPERTY: no container is ever lifted more than once, because a crane's lift can
only ever succeed while its token still matches the token currently stamped on that
container.
